question: A function $F(x)=x^3-2x+\sin x$ is an antiderivative of a function $f(x)$. Determine $\int \left[2f(x)+4x-\cos x\right]dx$ and verify the result by differentiation.
explanation:
Since $F(x)$ is an antiderivative of $f(x)$, integration and differentiation being inverse processes give

$$f(x)=F'(x)$$

Differentiating $F(x)=x^3-2x+\sin x$, we obtain

$$f(x)=3x^2-2+\cos x$$

Therefore,

$$2f(x)+4x-\cos x=2(3x^2-2+\cos x)+4x-\cos x$$

$$=6x^2+4x-4+\cos x$$

Hence,

$$\int \left[2f(x)+4x-\cos x\right]dx=\int \left(6x^2+4x-4+\cos x\right)dx$$

Integrating term by term,

$$=2x^3+2x^2-4x+\sin x+C$$

Verification

Differentiating the obtained expression,

$$\frac{d}{dx}\left(2x^3+2x^2-4x+\sin x+C\right)=6x^2+4x-4+\cos x$$

Also,

$$2f(x)+4x-\cos x=2(3x^2-2+\cos x)+4x-\cos x=6x^2+4x-4+\cos x$$

Thus, the differentiation reproduces the given integrand. Therefore, the required integral is $2x^3+2x^2-4x+\sin x+C$.
